Today in science we will learn about the life cycle — how animals grow and change from generation to generation.
A life cycle — the stages an animal goes through from start to adult:
Egg, then caterpillar, then chrysalis, and finally an adult butterfly.
Offspring are similar to their parents — a puppy looks like a dog, not like a cat.
Before that it was a caterpillar, and before that an egg on a leaf.
From the egg comes a small tadpole that breathes in water, and later it grows and becomes an adult frog that also breathes air.
Today in science we will learn about health and good habits — how to keep our body strong and happy.
Hygiene — washing hands before eating, brushing teeth in the morning and evening
Varied food and drink — fruits, vegetables, and water give the body energy
When we keep these habits — we feel better.
That way her body got rest, food, and cleanliness.
Before eating — so germs do not get into your mouth.
Before eating (and also after using the bathroom)
A child played in the garden and ate cookies without washing hands.
The next day they did not feel well.
What could they have done differently?
A child who ate without washing hands — what could they have done differently?
When you eat with dirty hands — germs get into your body and can make you sick.
Washing hands with soap before eating removes germs and keeps you healthy.
Today in science we will learn about the seasons of the year — and about the sun in the sky as a source of light and heat.
The sun — a star in the sky that gives light and heat.
At night — we do not see the sun in the sky; the moon and stars appear with weaker light.
Seasons change — but the sun is always the main source of light during the day.
In both seasons — during the day we see the sun in the sky.
What gives light and heat during the day?
During the day — it is bright and warm.
The light comes from the sun.
At night the sun is not visible from our side of Earth.
We see the moon and the stars.
The moon does not make its own light — it reflects some of the sun's light back to us.
Stars are very distant stars that shine on their own, but their light is weak from far away.
The answer: at night we see the moon and the stars. The moon reflects sunlight, and stars shine on their own.
When you practice, look for questions about summer, winter, and the source of light.
Today in science we will learn how to protect nature — less waste, more care for plants and animals.
Do not pick wildflowers without permission
Protecting nature — in the garden, at school, and in the park.
The children do not pick wildflowers — only in the allowed garden.
They use bins for paper and plastic, and do not disturb insects and birds.
That is how we protect nature — not just cleanliness, but care for life around us.
Why should we not pick wildflowers without permission?
Wildflowers in nature — food and shelter for insects and birds.
Birds build a nest to raise their chicks.
If we make loud noise or get too close — it can disturb the birds and the chicks.
Protecting nature also means not disturbing animals when they are raising their young.
When you practice, look for questions about waste and protecting the environment.
Today in science we will learn how to investigate like scientists — with observation, comparison, and one variable.
Observation — we look and describe (what is happening?)
Only the light changes — everything else is the same.
Write down what you see — without guessing.
If you change both water and light — you do not know what made the difference.
What will be the variable in this test?
What will be the variable in a test of a plant by a window versus a plant in a dark corner?
In a fair test you change only one thing — that is the variable.
The location (by a window with light versus a dark corner) is the only thing that changes.
The answer: the variable is the amount of light (the plant's location).
Today in science we will learn about states of matter — solid, liquid, and gas — in things we see every day.
This is a change you can see at home or in class — without a dangerous experiment.
In the air — gas that we breathe.
A cup of juice on the table — which state of matter?
A cup of juice — which state of matter?
Juice flows and takes the shape of the cup — that is a liquid.
A bottle that looks empty is full of air we cannot see — that is a gas.
A bottle that looks empty is full of air, which is a gas.
**Content scope:** Seed → plant; without water — does not grow
Today in science we will learn how a plant grows from a seed — and what happens when water is missing.
Without water — the seed does not sprout or the plant wilts.
If you forget to pour water — the plant does not grow well.
What happens to a seed without water?
Without water — the seed does not sprout, and therefore does not grow.
It does not sprout and does not grow.
Without light — the plant cannot make food, the leaves start to turn yellow and fall off.
The answer: the leaves will turn yellow and the plant will weaken.
Today in science we will learn how animals are adapted to the environment where they live.
We call this adaptation to the environment.
A habitat is the place where an animal finds food, water, and shelter.
Every animal has adaptations — features that help it survive:
Chameleon — body color that helps it blend into the environment (camouflage)
A tiger in a forest or thicket blends among the trees — color and markings help with camouflage.
Each animal has its own environment, and each has different adaptations.
Why does a fish have fins?
Which environment suits it?
Dense feathers create a layer of air that insulates its body from the cold.
Fat under the skin provides extra warmth and keeps body heat in.
The suitable environment — ice and cold water; the main adaptation — dense feathers and fat for warmth.
Every feature of the penguin's body is adapted to the extreme cold environment.
The skeleton is the structure of bones that supports the body and protects important organs.
You can think of the skeleton like a frame that supports the body, and muscles as parts that help us move.
The food passes through the mouth, esophagus, stomach, and intestines.
At the same time the muscles in her hands help her hold a cup — skeleton and muscles work together.
What is the role of the skeleton in the body?
Support and protection for the body
Bend your elbow — the muscles in your arm contract.
The bone in your arm stays straight — the skeleton holds the shape.
Which two parts are working here — skeleton or muscles?
The muscle in the arm contracts and pulls the bone upward.
The bones (skeleton) provide the frame and support for movement.
The skeleton gives support and structure. Muscles create movement. Together they allow every physical action.
When you practice, look for questions about the roles of body systems.
Weather — what happens in the sky today or this week:
Climate — the average weather over a long time (months and years) in an area.
The water cycle — water moves between the sea, sky, and land:
In the first stage, the sun heats water in the sea and some of it turns into vapor.
In the second stage, the vapor rises, cools, and condenses into tiny drops in clouds.
In the third stage, rain falls and the water returns to the sea and land.
In the fourth stage, plants, animals, and people use water — and the cycle continues.
Water from the sea evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain, flows in streams, and returns to the sea.
In Israel summers are usually hot and dry, and winters bring rain — a pattern like this over years is climate.
Rain falling today is weather.
A hot summer that returns here every year is part of the climate.
Where does water go after rain falls?
Rain is absorbed into the ground or flows in streams.
In the end most water returns to the sea.
What will happen to the puddle on a sunny day?
Where does the water go?
Which stage of the water cycle does it enter?
The water evaporates — goes from liquid to vapor that rises into the air.
The vapor cools and condenses into tiny drops in clouds — and so the water cycle continues.
The puddle water evaporates and rises into the air — that is the evaporation stage in the water cycle.
Evaporation — liquid water turns into vapor; then clouds form and rain falls.
When you practice, look for questions about rain, clouds, and the sea.
In every place in nature there are living things that depend on each other.
Which link in the chain?
In a chain where grass is eaten by a beetle, and the beetle is eaten by a bird, food flows like this:
Grass makes food with light — the beetle eats the grass — the bird feeds on the beetle.
Grass gives food to the beetle; the beetle gives food to the bird.
In this simple food chain — plant first, then herbivore, then predator.
Today in science we will learn how to plan a short experiment — with a hypothesis, observation, and one variable.
A scientific experiment tests a question about the world.
Variable — the only thing you change (for example amount of water).
According to the data — do the data support the hypothesis?
If you change several things — you do not know what made the difference.
Which plant is taller — by a window or in a corner?
In this experiment the only variable is light location (by a window or in a dark corner).
Only then can we know for sure that light location is the cause of the height change.
A fair experiment is one with only one variable, and all other conditions identical.
Today in science we will learn about forces — push and pull — and how they move objects.
A force is a push or pull that makes an object move or stop.
Friction is a force that resists motion when two surfaces touch.
A magnet can pull certain materials, like iron, without touching them.
Same push — different result because of the surface.
What happens when you stop pushing — why does the book stop?
Pushing a book on a table — you move the book away from you, that is a push force.
When you stop pushing, friction between the book and the table slows it down and stops it.
If no force keeps pushing, friction makes the book slow down and stop.
The force is a push; the book stops because of friction between the book and the table surface.
Today we will summarize what we learned in science about plants — the last lesson summary on this topic.
- Root — absorbs water and holds the plant in the ground
Inside the leaves, with the help of sunlight, the plant makes food for itself.
We call this making food: it is not food like humans eat, but the idea is similar.
Without enough light — the leaves start to pale and the plant weakens.
Input — light, water, and air; output — food for the plant.
Amount of water — even with light, without water the plant cannot make food properly.
In the light the plant makes food for itself.
Makes food with the help of light
Imagine a plant that grows for two weeks in a room with no window — no sunlight at all.
What will happen to food production in the plant?
Which growing condition is missing?
A plant without sunlight cannot make food inside its leaves.
Without food production — the plant weakens, the leaves lose their green color and turn pale.
Light is a necessary condition for making food; without it the plant cannot function.
The leaves will turn pale, the plant will weaken — the missing growing condition is sunlight.
Light, water, and suitable soil are important growing conditions; without light there is no food production in leaves.
When you practice, look for questions about plant needs and the role of the leaf.
Predator — an animal that eats another animal.
Two types of plants also compete for water in the same valley.
Who is the predator and who is the prey?
The question: a kingfisher and a small fish in a river — who is predator and who is prey? And there is also competition — for what?
A predator is an animal that feeds on other animals.
The kingfisher feeds on small fish — so it is the predator, and the small fish is the prey.
In a river, different kingfishers and other water birds compete for the same small fish as a food source.
Today in science we will learn about the respiratory system and the digestive system — how the body gets oxygen and breaks down food.
Breathing — when we breathe, air enters the lungs.
The lungs pass oxygen to the blood; the blood brings oxygen to the whole body.
The blood returns carbon dioxide to the lungs, and we breathe it out.
The mouth chews and moistens food, the esophagus carries it to the stomach, the stomach mixes it, and in the intestines nutrients are absorbed into the body.
Oxygen and nutrients from food help the body get energy for activity.
The body needs more oxygen for the muscles.
After a meal — digestion works in the stomach and intestines.
The body breaks down bread and vegetables into materials the blood carries.
Which gas enters the lungs when we breathe?
The lungs absorb oxygen into the blood.
Chew bread for a moment — notice your teeth and tongue.
Where does it go after swallowing?
The question: what happens to food in the mouth — and where does it go after swallowing?
After swallowing, food passes through the pharynx and esophagus to the stomach — where breakdown continues.
From the stomach it goes to the intestines, where nutrients are absorbed into the blood.
In the mouth — chewing and saliva. After swallowing — pharynx, esophagus, stomach, and intestines.
When you practice, look for questions about lungs, oxygen, and the path of food.
Today in science we will learn about rocks and soil — and how weather and seasons affect them.
Rain and sun change soil and rock throughout the year:
Earth is tilted — so different areas get different patterns of light and heat during the year (conceptual background).
In the mountains — exposed rocks; rain and wind encourage small cracks over time.
Same place — rock, soil, and water — change with the weather.
Plants need water and materials from the top layer.
Which material is rock?
Which is similar to soil?
The question: think about a beach — sand, rocks, water. Which material is rock? Which is similar to soil?
Rock is hard material formed in nature — a whole piece that does not break apart easily.
Sand forms when rocks break down over many years because of rain, wind, and waves — into small grains.
It is made of particles, and water passes through it — just like soil.
